## Post-2024 Transition: Retribution, Appointments, and Foreign Policy

In the weeks following his November 2024 election victory, Trump's repeated vows to seek revenge against political adversaries took on what The Hill described as a renewed seriousness, alarming those who had crossed him during his first term and the intervening years.[{n}] Reporting noted that after inauguration he would have new avenues to act on those calls and that he was assembling a team well positioned to carry out any retribution, including the nomination of former Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] as attorney general and the placement of several lawyers from his criminal defense team in senior Department of Justice posts.[{n}] House Republicans, having retained their majority, also vowed to investigate Trump adversaries.[{n}]

Badlands commentary framed Trump's campaign line "I will be your retribution" as one of his most misunderstood statements, arguing that its meaning was foreshadowed by his 2017 inaugural address, in which he described the transfer of power not from one administration or party to another but from Washington, D.C. back to the American people.[{n}] In this reading the first Trump administration, the intervening "Biden Pause," and the incoming second term formed a three-act strategy whose appointments had been decided long in advance.[{n}]

On November 19, 2024 Trump confirmed via Truth Social that he planned to declare a national emergency and use the U.S. military to carry out mass deportations, reposting a comment by Judicial Watch president [[tom-fitton|Tom Fitton]] with the caption "TRUE!!"[{n}] Estimates cited roughly 11 million undocumented immigrants in the United States, with the program expected to affect around 20 million families.[{n}]

During the same period Trump announced a rapid series of appointments: [[brendan-carr|Brendan Carr]] as Federal Communications Commission chairman, whom he called a "warrior for free speech"; [[linda-mcmahon|Linda McMahon]] as secretary of education, an agency he had vowed to abolish; [[howard-lutnick|Howard Lutnick]] as commerce secretary to lead a sweeping tariff program; and former congressman and Fox Business host [[sean-duffy|Sean Duffy]] as transportation secretary.[{n}] Trump praised Duffy as a "tremendous and well-liked public servant" and said he would eliminate DEI requirements for pilots and air traffic controllers.[{n}]

MSNBC "Morning Joe" hosts [[joe-scarborough|Joe Scarborough]] and [[mika-brzezinski|Mika Brzezinski]], long among his fiercest critics, traveled to Mar-a-Lago in mid-November 2024 to meet him and reopen lines of communication; Brzezinski described him as "cheerful, upbeat."[{n}] Trump was also photographed eating McDonald's aboard his plane with [[elon-musk|Elon Musk]], [[robert-f-kennedy-jr|Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]], Donald Trump Jr. and House Speaker [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] after a UFC event in New York City, an image that went viral and spawned a hoax claiming it had been predicted by a 1721 painting.[{n}]

On the legal front, a Georgia appeals court canceled December 5 oral arguments in Trump's bid to disqualify Fulton County District Attorney [[fani-willis|Fani Willis]], while New York prosecutors signaled in a court filing that they were open to postponing sentencing in his hush money case, potentially until the end of a second presidential term in 2029.[{n}] Trump's lawyers had urged Judge [[juan-merchan|Juan Merchan]] to dismiss the case outright "to facilitate the orderly transition of executive power."[{n}]
brendan-carr:
## Appointment as FCC Chairman and the "Censorship Cartel"

On November 17, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] announced Carr as his pick to lead the [[federal-communications-commission|Federal Communications Commission]], calling him a "warrior for free speech" and elevating him from the agency's senior Republican commissioner to permanent chairman.[{n}] Days before the announcement, in letters dated November 13, Carr had demanded answers from major technology firms about their participation in what he called a "censorship cartel" to suppress disfavored speech.[{n}]

The letters were addressed to Google's Sundar Pichai, Microsoft's Satya Nadella, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Apple's Tim Cook, and specifically sought information about the companies' dealings with [[newsguard|NewsGuard]], a for-profit "fact-checking" firm accused by congressional Republicans of labeling conservative outlets as riskier than liberal ones.[{n}] "Facebook, Google, Apple, Microsoft & others have played central roles in the censorship cartel," Carr wrote in an accompanying post on X. "The Orwellian named NewsGuard along with 'fact checking' groups & ad agencies helped enforce one-sided narratives."[{n}] The executives were directed to respond to the FCC by December 10 identifying which products or services partnered with NewsGuard and whether customers were required to rely on it.[{n}]

Badlands commentary welcomed the move, noting that Carr had targeted the same organization that had threatened numerous independent media outlets, including Badlands Media itself, and that [[mike-benz|Mike Benz]] had been publicizing NewsGuard's activities for months on X — a development framed as bad news for NewsGuard co-founder-linked figure [[jules-kroll|Jules Kroll]].[{n}]

## Carr Chairmanship and Big Tech Inquiry (2024)

In November 2024 President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] named senior Republican commissioner [[brendan-carr|Brendan Carr]] as permanent chairman of the commission, describing him as a "warrior for free speech."[{n}] Ahead of that announcement Carr used the agency's letterhead to press Google, Microsoft, Meta and Apple for information about their role in what he termed a "censorship cartel," and about their commercial relationships with the ratings firm [[newsguard|NewsGuard]], setting a December 10 deadline for responses.[{n}] The inquiry signaled that the commission under Carr would treat platform content moderation and third-party "fact-checking" partnerships as a central regulatory concern.[{n}]

## FCC Scrutiny Under Brendan Carr (2024)

In letters dated November 13, 2024, incoming [[federal-communications-commission|Federal Communications Commission]] chairman [[brendan-carr|Brendan Carr]] asked Google, Microsoft, Meta and Apple to disclose which of their products or services partnered with NewsGuard and whether customers were required to rely on it while using those services, with responses due by December 10.[{n}] Carr described NewsGuard as "Orwellian named" and said it, along with other fact-checking groups and ad agencies, had helped enforce one-sided narratives as part of a "censorship cartel."[{n}] The firm had already drawn criticism from congressional Republicans for allegedly labeling conservative outlets as more "risky" than liberal ones.[{n}] Badlands Media, which said it had itself been threatened by the organization, welcomed the scrutiny and credited [[mike-benz|Mike Benz]] with sustained public attention to the firm.[{n}]

## Nomination as Secretary of Education (2024)

On November 19, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] selected McMahon, his transition co-chair, to serve as secretary of the [[department-of-education|Department of Education]] — an agency he and his allies had pledged to abolish.[{n}] Then 76, McMahon had previously led the Small Business Administration during Trump's first term and was the former chief executive of [[world-wrestling-entertainment|World Wrestling Entertainment]], the company she built with her husband [[vince-mcmahon|Vince McMahon]].[{n}]

Trump said McMahon would use "decades of Leadership experience, and deep understanding of both Education and Business, to empower the next Generation of American Students and Workers," and indicated she would give states a larger role in education policy and pursue nationwide expansion of school choice.[{n}] He described her as a "fierce advocate for Parents' Rights" through her role as chairwoman of the America First Policy Institute.[{n}]

Badlands commentary noted that McMahon had described her WWE career in a speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention, that the promotion's highest-rated storylines of all time had involved Trump himself, and that she occasionally appeared as an on-screen character in its fictional universe.[{n}] The commentary also recalled that the McMahons' wrestling organization had helped fund Evel Knievel's failed Snake River Canyon jump, and that Linda left WWE in 2009 to run unsuccessfully for the U.S. Senate in Connecticut against [[richard-blumenthal|Richard Blumenthal]].[{n}]

## Nomination as Commerce Secretary (2024)

On November 19, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] chose Lutnick to serve as secretary of the [[department-of-commerce|Department of Commerce]] and to lead a sweeping program of tariffs, a role in which the department would be central to implementing the incoming administration's trade agenda.[{n}] Lutnick, a co-chair of Trump's transition, had hoped to become Treasury secretary, but Trump soured on the finalists for that post and began considering other options.[{n}]

Lutnick is chairman and chief executive of [[cantor-fitzgerald|Cantor Fitzgerald]], the investment firm he joined after graduating from college in the 1980s.[{n}] He became one of the most prominent business voices in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, when the firm's offices in the World Trade Center's North Tower were destroyed and hundreds of employees, including his brother, were killed.[{n}] He holds an annual fundraiser on September 11 for charities worldwide, and told the Wall Street Journal that having had to hire hundreds of replacement employees after 9/11 qualified him to help staff the incoming administration.[{n}]

Badlands commentary described Lutnick as a New York firebrand in Trump's own mold and a heterodox thinker inclined to go at the establishment rather than with it, and highlighted his standing as one of the first major Bitcoin advocates of the Wall Street class.[{n}]

## Lutnick's Move to Government (2024)

In November 2024 the firm's chairman and chief executive, [[howard-lutnick|Howard Lutnick]], was named President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s nominee for commerce secretary.[{n}] Lutnick had joined Cantor Fitzgerald after graduating from college in the 1980s and rose to lead it.[{n}] The firm's offices occupied the North Tower of the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, and hundreds of its employees — among them Lutnick's brother — were killed; Lutnick subsequently rebuilt the staff and established an annual September 11 charity fundraiser.[{n}]

## Attorney General Nomination and Senate Resistance (2024)

After the 2024 election, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] nominated Gaetz, then a Republican representative from Florida, to serve as attorney general, a choice reported alongside the placement of several of Trump's criminal defense lawyers in other senior Department of Justice posts.[{n}] The pick was widely read as part of Trump's stated intention to pursue retribution against political adversaries.[{n}]

By November 19, 2024, numerous Republican senators had told Trump and his team that they believed Gaetz had little chance of being confirmed, a message delivered to the president-elect himself, to incoming White House chief of staff [[susie-wiles|Susie Wiles]], and to Gaetz's unofficial "sherpa," Vice President-elect [[jd-vance|JD Vance]].[{n}] Senators worried about being tarnished by the process; those facing reelection in 2026, including [[thom-tillis|Thom Tillis]], feared a MAGA primary challenge if they opposed the nomination and a general-election liability if they backed it.[{n}] Others argued that Trump would waste political capital and attention on confirmation hearings better spent dismantling Joe Biden's regulatory and legislative legacy.[{n}] Trump reportedly acknowledged that Gaetz had "less than even odds" of confirmation but still wanted a fight, asking Republican senators to give his pick "a shot" and arguing that Gaetz was the man to fix the Justice Department, according to Sen. [[kevin-cramer|Kevin Cramer]].[{n}]

## Chief of Staff and the Gaetz Nomination (2024)

As incoming White House chief of staff, Wiles was one of the figures to whom Senate Republicans privately conveyed their view that [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] had little chance of being confirmed as attorney general in November 2024, alongside President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] himself and Vice President-elect [[jd-vance|JD Vance]].[{n}]

Following the 2024 election, Vance served as the unofficial "sherpa" guiding [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]]'s nomination for attorney general through the Senate.[{n}] Republican senators skeptical of the nomination delivered their doubts directly to Vance, as well as to President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] and incoming chief of staff [[susie-wiles|Susie Wiles]].[{n}]

## Appeals Court Cancels Disqualification Arguments (2024)

On November 18, 2024, the Georgia Court of Appeals canceled oral arguments scheduled for December 5 in President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s bid to disqualify Willis from prosecuting him, issuing a one-sentence order with no explanation that postponed the hearing "until further order of this Court."[{n}] The cancellation came less than two weeks after Trump's election victory.[{n}] Trump had sought to derail the Fulton County prosecution over his attempt to overturn the 2020 Georgia election result by challenging Willis's relationship with [[nathan-wade|Nathan Wade]], the top prosecutor she hired to oversee the case; the trial judge allowed the case to proceed on the condition that Wade resign, which he did.[{n}] The appeals court had been set to hear arguments from Trump and eight co-defendants that Willis could not continue to oversee the prosecution.[{n}]

## Aftermath in the Georgia Appeal (2024)

The disqualification fight arising from Wade's relationship with Fulton County District Attorney [[fani-willis|Fani Willis]] continued into the appellate stage after his resignation, but on November 18, 2024, the Georgia Court of Appeals canceled the December 5 oral arguments in [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s disqualification bid without explanation.[{n}]

## Hush Money Sentencing After the 2024 Election

Merchan postponed a sentencing hearing set for November 26, 2024, in the New York hush money case following [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s reelection.[{n}] In a filing on November 19, 2024, prosecutors suggested they were open to postponing sentencing further, acknowledging that "consideration must be given" to pausing the case until the end of Trump's second presidential term in 2029.[{n}] Trump's lawyers had urged Merchan to throw the case out entirely "to facilitate the orderly transition of executive power" and had also requested a new trial, a decision on which remained pending.[{n}]

## Nomination as Transportation Secretary (2024)

On November 18, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] announced Duffy, a former congressman and recent Fox Business co-host, as his choice to lead the Department of Transportation.[{n}] Duffy had served in the U.S. House from 2011 to 2019 representing Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, and most recently co-hosted Fox Business's "The Bottom Line" after joining Fox News as a contributor in 2020; his last day as a Fox News employee was the Monday of the announcement.[{n}] Trump praised him as a "tremendous and well-liked public servant" and "a respected voice and communicator in the Republican Conference," saying he would prioritize "Excellence, Competence, Competitiveness and Beauty" in rebuilding highways, tunnels, bridges and airports, ensure ports and dams served the economy without compromising national security, and "make our skies safe again by eliminating DEI for pilots and air traffic controllers."[{n}]

## Mar-a-Lago Meeting with Trump (2024)

Two weeks after the 2024 election, Scarborough and his co-host and wife [[mika-brzezinski|Mika Brzezinski]] traveled to Mar-a-Lago to meet President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], saying they wished to reopen lines of communication that would better serve their morning show's viewers.[{n}] The trip drew criticism from both fans and detractors of "Morning Joe," given how sharply the program had attacked Trump — in September 2024 Scarborough said it was "not a reach" to compare him to Hitler, and [[msnbc|MSNBC]] pulled the show off the air the Monday after the summer assassination attempt on Trump.[{n}] The hosts said they reached out on a Thursday and met Trump the following day, the first time they had seen him in seven years.[{n}]

## Mar-a-Lago Meeting with Trump (2024)

Brzezinski and co-host [[joe-scarborough|Joe Scarborough]] met President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] at his Florida home in November 2024 to restart communications after years of hostile coverage.[{n}] She said it was the first time they had seen him in seven years and described him as "cheerful, upbeat" even as the three discussed points of disagreement.[{n}] "What we did agree on was to restart communications," she said, likening the effort to the practice of her father, the late Zbigniew Brzezinski, national security adviser in Jimmy Carter's administration, who often spoke with world leaders he disagreed with.[{n}]

## Viral McDonald's Photograph (2024)

In November 2024 Musk appeared in a widely circulated photograph eating McDonald's aboard [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s plane alongside Trump, [[robert-f-kennedy-jr|Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]] and Donald Trump Jr., with House Speaker [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] standing in the background, taken after the group attended a UFC event in New York City.[{n}] The image was posted by Trump deputy communications director Margo Martin and went viral; when X user @boneGPT reposted it beside an image falsely described as a 1721 painting by "Deitz Nuützen" that had predicted the scene, Musk replied with a laughing emoji, and the post was viewed 4.3 million times within two days.[{n}] Newsweek rated the claim false, finding no evidence of such an 18th-century painter and concluding the image was almost certainly AI-generated as a "deez nuts" joke.[{n}]

## Reported Use Against Russian Territory (November 2024)

On Tuesday, November 19, 2024, the Kremlin said Ukraine had fired six U.S.-made long-range missiles into Russian territory, of which Russia shot down five and damaged the sixth; Ukraine did not confirm that it had fired ATACMS.[{n}] The strikes followed President Joe Biden's decision to authorize the launch of U.S.-made missiles into Russia, a move Russian officials warned could lead to a world war.[{n}] Badlands commentary characterized the episode as a "budding Ukrainian Missile Crisis" and a rerun of the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, arguing it followed a pre-seeded narrative template and would create crisis points allowing [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] to assume the role of peacemaker before taking office.[{n}]
